title: Diffusion language models: generating text by unmasking
summary: How masked diffusion LMs like LLaDA and Mercury generate text by iteratively unmasking tokens in parallel: the masking process, the likelihood-bound loss, remasking samplers, and the speed tradeoffs.
outcomes: Explain how a masked diffusion LM's forward masking process and its exact reverse define a generative model, and derive the s/t step
Compute the masked diffusion training loss for a sequence and explain why it weights by 1/t
Turn a GPT into a masked diffusion LM, train it, sample from it and compare its likelihood bound with the AR model's exact loss
Trace low-confidence remasking step by step and predict how many tokens each step commits
Explain why parallel unmasking breaks token dependencies and when a confidence threshold makes it safe
Estimate when a decode pass is memory-bound and compare diffusion and autoregressive LMs on passes, compute, caching and quality
Explain how AR initialization, diffu-GRPO, variance-reduced DPO and remasking samplers make diffusion LMs practical

lessons.title: Why generate text in any order other than left to right?

blocks.md: The GPT you built is an **autoregressive model (ARM)**: it factorizes the probability of a sequence as a product of next-token conditionals, $p_\theta(x) = \prod_i p_\theta(x^i \mid x^1, \dots, x^{i-1})$. Training is parallel thanks to teacher forcing (the true earlier tokens are fed in as input, so every position's next-token prediction is trained in the same pass), but generation is not. To produce 256 tokens the model must run 256 forward passes one after another, because token 257 cannot be predicted until token 256 exists.

Each of those decode passes does very little arithmetic per weight it reads: one new token per sequence goes through the whole network. With a **KV cache** (the stored keys and values of earlier tokens, so they are not recomputed) the work per pass is small, and the GPU spends most of its time moving weights from memory rather than computing. Latency is set by the number of sequential passes.

The left-to-right order has two other costs. A token, once emitted, is never revised. And the model only ever learns conditionals in one direction. The **reversal curse** (Berglund et al., 2023) is the classic symptom: a model trained on "A is B" often fails to answer "what is B?" with A.

scenes.caption: An autoregressive model emits one token per forward pass. Eight tokens need eight passes in strict order, no matter how big the GPU is.
A masked diffusion model starts from 8 mask tokens and, in each pass, predicts every masked position at once. Here 4 steps each commit 2 tokens: half as many sequential passes.
Side by side. Simplified: without a KV cache, each diffusion pass recomputes the whole sequence, so it is more work per pass. Fewer passes only wins when the GPU has spare compute.

blocks.md: **Diffusion models** take a different route, proven first on images. A fixed **forward process** gradually corrupts data with noise until nothing is left; a network learns the **reverse process** that removes noise a little at a time. Generation starts from pure noise and refines the whole sample over a chosen number of steps.

For text, the most successful noise has turned out to be the simplest: replace tokens with a special **[MASK]** token. Austin et al. (D3PM, short for Discrete Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Models, 2021) called this an **absorbing state**, because once a token becomes [MASK] it stays masked for the rest of the forward process. Models built on it are **masked diffusion models (MDMs)**. Generation then means: start with all positions masked and repeatedly fill some in.

blocks.title: Which positions each token may attend to

scenes.caption: Your GPT uses a causal mask: row i (the query) may only see columns up to i. Position 3 cannot look at 'on' or 'mat' when it is predicted.
A mask predictor drops the causal mask. Every position sees every other position, so the masked slot at position 3 can use both 'cat' on its left and 'on' and 'mat' on its right.

blocks.md: This course follows **LLaDA** (Nie et al., 2025; the name stands for Large Language Diffusion with mAsking), an 8-billion-parameter masked diffusion model trained from scratch. Its starting point is the goal every language model shares: **maximum likelihood**, making the training texts as probable as possible. That is the same as minimizing the **Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence** from the data distribution to the model, the expected value over real text of $\log p_{\text{data}}(x) - \log p_\theta(x)$: a measure of how much worse the model predicts real text than the data distribution itself, which is zero only when the two match. The first term does not depend on $\theta$, so lowering the KL means raising the expected $\log p_\theta(x)$.

blocks.caption: The generative modeling principle. LLaDA's argument: scaling, **in-context learning** (picking up a task from examples in the prompt) and instruction following come from maximizing likelihood with a big Transformer, not from the left-to-right factorization itself.

blocks.md: A diffusion language model keeps the Transformer and the maximum-likelihood goal of a GPT. It changes two things: attention is bidirectional, and generation fills in many masked positions per step in any order instead of one token at the end.

A masked diffusion LM is not just BERT (Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers, Devlin et al., 2018), the bidirectional Transformer pretrained to fill in masked words. BERT masks a fixed 15% of tokens and has no way to sample a whole text. A masked diffusion LM trains on every masking ratio from 0 to 1 with a loss that bounds the likelihood, which is exactly what makes generation from an all-mask sequence possible.

blocks.prompt: LLaDA can generate a 256-token answer in 64 steps. How many sequential forward passes is that, and how many tokens does each pass process if the prompt is 894 tokens?
blocks.reveal: 64 sequential passes instead of 256. But LLaDA has no KV cache, so each pass processes the full prompt plus the full answer: 894 + 256 = 1150 tokens. An autoregressive model with a cache processes those 1150 tokens about once in total. Diffusion trades **more total compute** for **fewer sequential steps**, which pays off when decoding is memory-bound. The next figure puts numbers on that.

blocks.md: How memory-bound is a decode pass? Take an 8B model stored in bfloat16 (2 bytes per weight): every forward pass reads 16 GB of weights. Each token pushed through the pass costs about 2 FLOPs per weight (a multiply and an add), so one token does 16 GFLOP of work for 16 GB read, about **1 FLOP per byte**. An NVIDIA H100 SXM lists 1,979 TFLOP/s of bfloat16 math with sparsity, so about 989.5 TFLOP/s dense (half that figure), and 3.35 TB/s of memory bandwidth, a ratio of about 295 FLOPs per byte. So the 16 GB read takes 4.8 ms, and a pass can carry up to about 295 tokens before the arithmetic takes longer than the read. Below that, extra tokens per pass are nearly free. The numbers come from the [H100 datasheet](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/data-center/h100/); the ratio is called the ridge point: above it a pass is limited by arithmetic, below it by memory traffic.

blocks.title: Idealized time for a 256-token answer on one H100 (64 steps)

scenes.caption: Batch 1, 8B model, each pass costing max(memory time, math time). AR: 256 passes of 4.8 ms. No-cache diffusion pushes 1150 tokens per pass, 18.6 ms of math, so it is already compute-bound and only ties. 32-token passes stay memory-bound.

Batch 64: the AR pass now carries 64 tokens and is still memory-bound, so 64 answers cost the same 1.22 s. Diffusion multiplies its tokens per pass by 64 and pays every FLOP: 76.2 s without a cache, 2.12 s with 32-token passes.

blocks.md: Simplified: these are lower bounds that ignore attention FLOPs, reading the KV cache, the prompt's prefill and kernel overheads, and the 32-token case assumes a step only recomputes its own block (lesson 6 shows the approximate cache that makes this possible). The shape of the result is what matters. At batch 1 the GPU has hundreds of tokens of spare compute per pass, and diffusion spends it on parallel unmasking. At serving batches the AR decode fills that spare compute with other users' tokens, and diffusion's recomputation is paid in full.

blocks.question: Why is autoregressive decoding slow on a GPU even though the GPU can do far more arithmetic per second than one token needs?
options: Each step must wait for the previous token, and each step does little compute per byte of weights read, so the GPU idles on memory traffic
Softmax over the vocabulary is the dominant cost and cannot be parallelized
The KV cache makes every step recompute attention over all earlier tokens from scratch
Causal attention needs more FLOPs than bidirectional attention
blocks.explain: Decode is sequential (token t+1 needs token t) and memory-bound: each pass streams all weights to process one token per sequence. A KV cache avoids recomputation; it does not create it. Causal attention actually computes fewer scores than bidirectional attention.

blocks.question: What does the 'absorbing state' in masked diffusion refer to?
options: The final layer of the Transformer that absorbs all positional information
The [MASK] token: once the forward process masks a token, it stays masked
The end-of-sequence token that stops generation
A Gaussian noise vector added to token embeddings
blocks.explain: In D3PM's absorbing-state process every token moves to [MASK] at some point and never leaves it. At the final time the sequence is entirely masked, which gives a simple known starting point for generation.

lessons.title: The forward process: masking as noise, and its exact reverse

blocks.md: Let $x_0$ be a clean training sequence of length $L$ and let the **time** $t$ run from 0 to 1. The forward process produces a partly masked copy $x_t$: every token is replaced by [MASK] (written M) independently with probability $t$, and kept with probability $1-t$. At $t=0$ nothing is masked; at $t=1$ everything is.

blocks.tex: q_{t|0}(x_t^i \mid x_0^i) = \begin{cases} 1 - t, & x_t^i = x_0^i \\ t, & x_t^i = \mathrm{M} \end{cases} \qquad q_{t|0}(x_t \mid x_0) = \prod_{i=1}^{L} q_{t|0}(x_t^i \mid x_0^i)
blocks.caption: LLaDA's forward process (its Eq. 7 and 8). The masking probability grows linearly in t, on the reasoning that information in text is roughly proportional to the number of tokens.

blocks.title: One sentence moving through the forward process

scenes.caption: t = 0: the clean sentence. Each token gets one uniform random number u (computed with a seeded generator); a token is masked at time t when its u is below t.
t = 0.25: tokens with u < 0.25 are masked. That is 3 of 8, while the expected count is tL = 2. The count itself is random.
t = 0.5: 'sat' (u = 0.28) joins the masks, giving 4 of 8. Reusing the same draws makes the masks nest, which is a simplification for display; each t is still marginally correct.
t = 0.75: 7 of 8 masked. Only 'today' (u = 0.89) survives. The model at this noise level sees almost no context.
t = 1: every token is masked. This all-mask sequence is the known starting point of generation, the text analogue of pure Gaussian noise for images.

blocks.md: Because each token is masked independently, the number masked is Binomial($L$, $t$): the count of heads in $L$ coin flips that each land heads with probability $t$. Its mean is $tL$, but for a short sequence the spread is large. This matters later: it is why LLaDA evaluates likelihoods by masking an exact count of tokens instead.

blocks.title: How many of 8 tokens get masked?

scenes.caption: t = 0.5: the most likely count is 4, but only with probability 0.273. Counts 3 to 5 together cover 0.711.
t = 0.25: centred on 2 (probability 0.311), and there is a 0.1 chance that nothing at all is masked, which gives no training signal.

blocks.md: To generate we must run time backwards. For two times $0 \le s < t \le 1$, the exact reverse of this forward process factorizes over positions too. A token that is already visible stays as it is. A masked token stays masked with probability $s/t$, and otherwise is revealed with probability $(t-s)/t$, its value drawn from $q_{0|t}$, the distribution of the clean token given what is visible.

blocks.tex: q_{s|t}(x_s^i \mid x_t) = \begin{cases} 1, & x_t^i \ne \mathrm{M},\ x_s^i = x_t^i \\ \frac{s}{t}, & x_t^i = \mathrm{M},\ x_s^i = \mathrm{M} \\ \frac{t-s}{t}\, q_{0|t}(x_s^i \mid x_t), & x_t^i = \mathrm{M},\ x_s^i \ne \mathrm{M} \\ 0, & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}
blocks.caption: The reverse step (LLaDA Eq. 10). Everything is known in closed form except q, the prediction of the original token at a masked position. That one function is what the neural network learns.

blocks.md: Where does $s/t$ come from? Give every token a **masking time** $\tau$, drawn uniformly between 0 and 1, and say the token is masked at time $t$ exactly when $\tau < t$. That reproduces the forward process, since $P(\tau < t) = t$, and it is how the first figure was drawn: each draw $u$ is a masking time. Now suppose a token is masked at $t$. All we learn is $\tau < t$, so $\tau$ is equally likely to be anywhere below $t$. The token is still masked at the earlier time $s$ exactly when $\tau < s$, which has probability $s/t$.

blocks.tex: P(x_s^i = \mathrm{M} \mid x_t^i = \mathrm{M}) = P(\tau < s \mid \tau < t) = \frac{P(\tau < s)}{P(\tau < t)} = \frac{s}{t}
blocks.caption: Bayes' rule. The joint event 'masked at s and at t' is just 'masked at s', because tau < s already implies tau < t.

blocks.md: Otherwise $\tau$ fell between $s$ and $t$: the token was visible at $s$. The forward process never turns a token into a different word, so a visible token at $s$ must be the clean token $x_0^i$. The reverse step does not know $x_0^i$, so it draws it from $q_{0|t}$, which gives the third line of the formula with weight $1 - s/t = (t-s)/t$.

blocks.title: Masking times explain the s/t rule

scenes.caption: At t = 0.5 the four tokens with masking time below 0.5 are hidden. Seen from inside the reverse process, each of their times is now equally likely to be anywhere in [0, 0.5).
Step to s = 0.25. Each hidden token stays hidden if its time is below 0.25, with probability 0.25 / 0.5 = 0.5. Here 'cat' (0.03), 'on' (0.22) and '.' (0.09) qualify.
'sat' (0.28) had its time between s and t, so it is revealed, and it can only come back as 'sat'. The expected count is 0.5 x 4 = 2 revealed; this draw revealed 1. The randomness is real.

blocks.md: There is a further simplification. The visible tokens in $x_t$ are just copies of tokens in $x_0$, and which ones survived carries no information about the hidden ones. So $q_{0|t}(x^i \mid x_t) = p_{\text{data}}(x_0^i \mid x_t^{\text{UM}})$, where $x_t^{\text{UM}}$ is the set of unmasked tokens. The time $t$ drops out, and the network does not need $t$ as an input (proved by Ou et al. and restated in LLaDA's appendix).

MDLM (Sahoo et al., 2024) builds these facts into the network as the **SUBS parameterization**, named for the two substitutions it makes in the network's output: the logit of [MASK] is set to minus infinity, so the model never predicts a mask (**zero masking probabilities**), and any visible input token is copied to the output unchanged (**carry-over unmasking**). Both simplify the training loss of lesson 3, which is a bound on the likelihood. On LM1B (the One Billion Word benchmark of news sentences) and measured in perplexity (e raised to the average loss per token, the number of equally likely choices the model is effectively torn between; lower is better), carry-over unmasking is worth about 1.5 perplexity points, while zero masking makes no meaningful difference.

The forward process is fixed and trivial. The only thing to learn is a **mask predictor**: given a partly masked sequence, output a distribution over the vocabulary at every masked position. It needs no timestep input.

blocks.prompt: A reverse step goes from t = 0.5 to s = 0.25 on a sequence with 4 masked tokens. Under the exact reverse process, how many tokens do you expect to be revealed, and can a visible token change?
blocks.reveal: Each masked token stays masked with probability $s/t = 0.25/0.5 = 0.5$, so on average 2 of the 4 are revealed. Visible tokens are carried over with probability 1, so in this basic sampler a committed token never changes. That is the absorbing property running backwards.

blocks.question: Why can the mask predictor ignore the time t?
options: Because t is always 0.5 during training
Because the visible tokens are exact copies of the clean ones, so the best prediction of a hidden token depends only on what is visible, not on how much noise was applied
Because the Transformer's positional encoding already contains t
It cannot; LLaDA concatenates t to every token embedding
blocks.explain: The posterior of a masked token given x_t equals the data conditional given the unmasked tokens, which is time-invariant. The number of visible tokens already reflects the noise level, so feeding t adds nothing. MDLM also reports similar perplexity with and without time conditioning.

blocks.question: In a reverse step from t to s, a masked position stays masked with probability s/t. What happens when s = 0?
options: Every masked position is revealed in this step
Nothing is revealed, because s/t = 0 means no change
Half of the masked positions are revealed
The visible tokens are remasked
blocks.explain: With s = 0 the probability of staying masked is 0/t = 0, so every remaining mask must be filled. The last step of any schedule ends at s = 0 and finishes the sequence.

lessons.title: Training: a weighted average of masked-LM losses

blocks.md: The mask predictor is a Transformer like your GPT, with RMSNorm, SwiGLU and RoPE in LLaDA's case, but with **no causal mask**. These are the usual modern swaps: RMSNorm scales each vector by its root mean square instead of subtracting the mean and dividing by the standard deviation as LayerNorm does; SwiGLU is a feed-forward layer where one linear projection, passed through the Swish activation, gates a second projection elementwise; RoPE (rotary position embedding) rotates pairs of query and key dimensions by an angle proportional to the position, so attention scores depend on how far apart two tokens are. It takes a partly masked sequence and outputs logits at every position. Training is one line different from BERT, and that line is what turns a fill-in-the-blank model into a generative model.

The bidirectional Transformer sees x_t (masked and visible tokens together) and predicts a token distribution at every position in one pass.

blocks.title: Worked example: the loss for one sequence at t = 0.5

scenes.caption: The sentence from lesson 2 at t = 0.5: positions 2, 3, 4 and 8 are masked. Those four are the only positions that will be scored.
The model's probability for the correct token at each masked slot (toy values chosen for illustration). '.' at the end is easy; 'cat' has many plausible alternatives.
Negative log-probabilities, computed: 1.204 + 0.799 + 0.511 + 0.105 = 2.619. Visible positions add zero.
Divide by t L = 0.5 x 8 = 4: the loss is 2.619 / 4 = 0.655. Four masked tokens, so this is the average per masked token.

blocks.md: Now take the same sentence at t = 0.25, where 3 tokens are masked ('cat', 'on', '.'). With more context the model is more confident: say probabilities 0.40, 0.70 and 0.95. The summed loss is only 1.324, but the divisor is also smaller, t L = 2, so the loss is 0.662. The $1/t$ factor rescales each noise level by the number of tokens it is expected to mask, $tL$.

blocks.title: Why the 1/t weight

scenes.caption: On average a fraction t of tokens is masked, so the raw sum of masked losses scales with t.
Weighting by 1/t blows up at small t, where only a few tokens are masked.
Their product is 1 at every t: each noise level gets equal say in the objective, measured per masked token. This weighting is what makes the loss a bound on likelihood.

blocks.md: This weighting is not a heuristic. Shi et al., Sahoo et al. (MDLM) and Ou et al. proved that $\mathcal{L}(\theta)$ is an **upper bound on the negative log-likelihood**, $-\mathbb{E}\log p_\theta(x_0) \le \mathcal{L}(\theta)$. MDLM describes it as a weighted average of masked-language-modeling losses. MaskGIT (Masked Generative Image Transformer, Chang et al., 2022), which draws images by repeatedly unmasking image tokens, used a similar objective without the $1/t$ factor, which loses the link to maximum likelihood; BERT uses a single fixed ratio and so never learns the nearly-all-masked regime that generation starts from.

Here is where the $1/t$ comes from. Split generation into many small reverse steps from $t$ to $s$. The bound charges each step for the tokens it reveals: a masked token is revealed with probability $(t-s)/t$ (lesson 2), and revealing it costs $-\log p_\theta(x_0^i \mid x_t)$, how surprised the model is by the true token. So one step costs $(t-s)/t$ times the summed masked losses. With a tiny step $t - s = dt$ the weight is $dt/t$, and adding up every step from $t = 1$ down to 0 gives an integral over $t$ of $1/t$ times the masked loss, which is exactly drawing $t$ uniformly and weighting by $1/t$. The total is an upper bound, not the exact value, for the usual diffusion reason: the exact likelihood sums the probability of every path from all-masked to clean text, the loss instead averages the log-probability along random paths drawn from the forward process, and by Jensen's inequality (the log of an average is at least the average of the logs) that can only overestimate the negative log-likelihood.

blocks.code:
def mdm_loss(model, x0, mask_id):
    # x0: (B, L) token ids
    B, L = x0.shape
    t = torch.rand(B, 1).clamp_min(1e-3)         # one noise level per sequence
    masked = torch.rand(B, L) < t                # mask each token with prob t
    xt = torch.where(masked, mask_id, x0)
    logits = model(xt)                           # bidirectional, no t input
    ce = F.cross_entropy(logits.transpose(1, 2), x0, reduction='none')  # (B, L)
    return ((ce * masked) / t).sum() / (B * L)   # only masked tokens, weight 1/t
blocks.caption: A minimal PyTorch version of LLaDA's Algorithm 1 (the loss is divided by t L per sequence, then averaged over the batch).

blocks.md: **Fine-tuning** keeps the same loss. For a prompt and response pair, only response tokens are masked; the prompt stays visible. LLaDA pads short responses in a batch with end-of-sequence tokens (|EOS|) and trains on them like any token, so the model learns to end its answer by filling the tail with |EOS|.

**Evaluating likelihood** (for multiple-choice benchmarks) uses an equivalent form with lower variance: draw a count $l$ uniformly from 1 to $L$, mask exactly $l$ tokens, and weight by $L/l$. That weight is the $1/t$ of the main loss in disguise: masking exactly $l$ of $L$ tokens is noise level $t = l/L$, so $1/t = L/l$. LLaDA reports that the independent-masking form needs over 1000 Monte Carlo samples (independent random maskings averaged together) for stable results while the exact-count form needs 128, because it removes the binomial spread you saw in lesson 2.

Perplexities reported for diffusion LMs are usually upper bounds (written as a less-or-equal sign in the papers), not exact values. Comparing a bound to an autoregressive model's exact perplexity slightly favours the autoregressive model.

blocks.question: Spot the bug: a colleague's loss is `(ce * masked).sum() / masked.sum()`, the plain average over masked tokens, with t still drawn uniformly. What changes?
options: Nothing; it is the same quantity
The loss now includes visible tokens

Summed over the batch and divided by the total masked count, every masked token gets equal weight, so heavily masked sequences dominate; the 1/t factor is lost and it is no longer the likelihood bound
The model will learn to predict [MASK] tokens
blocks.explain: Over a large batch the ratio tends to E[sum of masked losses] / E[count]: the unweighted MaskGIT-style objective with no 1/t, which LLaDA notes lacks a link to maximum likelihood. The principled loss divides each sequence by t L. Dividing each sequence by its own masked count would actually be fine: with uniform t the count is uniform on 0 to L, which is the exact-count form LLaDA uses for likelihoods (skip sequences with nothing masked).

blocks.question: Why does training on t drawn from all of [0, 1] matter for generation, compared with BERT's fixed 15%?
options: Generation starts from a fully masked sequence, so the model must be good at predicting with almost no context; a fixed 15% ratio never trains that regime
Uniform t makes training cheaper per step
It lets the model use a causal mask
It removes the need for a tokenizer
blocks.explain: Sampling walks t from 1 down to 0, visiting every masking ratio. A model that only ever saw 15% masks has never learned the early, nearly empty steps, and its loss is not a likelihood bound.

lessons.title: Sampling: predict every mask, keep the confident, remask the rest

blocks.md: Generation runs the reverse process with $N$ discrete steps. Fix a response length $L$, fill it with [MASK], and step time from $t = 1$ down to 0 in increments of $1/N$. At each step from $t$ to $s = t - 1/N$, one forward pass predicts every masked position, and then a fraction $s/t$ of the newly predicted tokens is put back to [MASK] so that the expected number of masks matches the forward process at time $s$.

Which tokens get remasked? The exact reverse process says: a random subset (LLaDA's Algorithm 4, **random remasking**). LLaDA's default instead uses **low-confidence remasking** (Algorithm 5, taken from MaskGIT): it scores each prediction by its probability, keeps the most confident, and remasks the rest. After the step from t to s, floor(L(1 - s)) positions are unmasked; tokens already committed get confidence 1 and are never remasked.

blocks.title: Low-confidence remasking: 8 tokens in 4 steps

scenes.caption: The prompt asks for the capital of France; the response is 8 positions, all [MASK], and we will use N = 4 steps. The response length is a hyperparameter fixed before sampling starts.
Step 1 (t = 1 to s = 0.75): one forward pass predicts all 8 positions. Keep floor(8 x (1 - 0.75)) = 2. The two |EOS| slots at the end are the most confident, so they are committed first.
Step 2 (s = 0.5): committed tokens count as confidence 1, so keep 4 in total: the two |EOS| plus position 6 (|EOS|, 0.96) and 'Paris' (0.88). Every other prediction is thrown away and remasked.
Step 3 (s = 0.25): keep 6. 'is' (0.93) and '.' (0.91) now beat 'The' (0.62), because the model can see 'Paris' and the end of the answer.
Step 4 (s = 0): keep all 8. The answer is 'The city is Paris .' and the |EOS| tokens are stripped. Four passes for eight tokens.

blocks.md: The confidences in the figure are illustrative, but the order they produce is the real behaviour LLaDA reports. Because supervised fine-tuning pads answers with |EOS|, the instruct model becomes very confident about |EOS| at the tail. Under pure diffusion this produced too many |EOS| tokens and very short answers, so for several benchmarks the authors set the confidence of |EOS| to zero during sampling. LLaDA comes as a Base model (pre-training only) and an Instruct model (after supervised fine-tuning, SFT). The benchmark quoted most below is GSM8K (Grade School Math 8K, Cobbe et al., 2021): about 8,500 grade-school math word problems, scored by whether the final answer is right. The next figure also uses BBH (BIG-Bench Hard, 23 hard reasoning tasks), Math (defined below) and two code tests checked by unit tests: HumanEval (164 Python functions) and MBPP (Mostly Basic Python Problems, short tasks).

scenes.caption: The response starts as L masks after the prompt.
Step 1 runs from t = 1 to s = 0.75.
A single forward pass scores every position. Greedy argmax is LLaDA's default (temperature 0).

blocks.md: **Steps trade quality for speed.** With a 256-token answer, 256 steps reveal one token per pass; 64 steps reveal four per pass. LLaDA's paper shows quality falling as tokens per pass rise, and on GSM8K and Math (the MATH benchmark of 12,500 competition math problems, Hendrycks et al., 2021) its 8B base model matched the accuracy of LLaMA3 8B, Meta's 8-billion-parameter autoregressive model, at 1.5 and 1.8 times the throughput, without any caching.

**Semi-autoregressive (block) sampling** splits the answer into blocks, runs the diffusion steps inside one block at a time, and moves left to right across blocks. In the official `generate.py` this is the `block_length` argument (the mask token id is 126336). For LLaDA 8B Instruct, block sampling lifted GSM8K from 69.4 to 78.6 with block length 8, because it stops |EOS| from being committed at the tail too early.

A sampling step is: one forward pass over the whole sequence, a guess at every masked slot, then keep the k most confident guesses and remask the rest. The schedule fixes k per step; the confidence ranking decides the order.

blocks.question: With L = 256 and N = 32 steps, how many tokens are committed per forward pass on average, and how many passes are needed?
options: 1 token per pass, 256 passes
8 tokens per pass, 32 passes
32 tokens per pass, 8 passes
It depends on the prompt length
blocks.explain: The linear schedule spreads 256 unmaskings evenly over 32 steps: 256 / 32 = 8 per pass, 32 passes in total. That is the 8-tokens-per-pass point in LLaDA's sampling-efficiency figure.

blocks.question: LLaDA 8B Instruct, under pure diffusion sampling, gives very short answers on math benchmarks. What is the most likely cause?
options: The model was trained with a causal mask
The response length hyperparameter was set too large
Random remasking was used by default
Fine-tuning data padded with |EOS| makes tail |EOS| predictions highly confident, so low-confidence remasking commits them first
blocks.explain: Padding teaches the model that the tail is |EOS|, and low-confidence remasking commits the most confident tokens first. The fixes LLaDA used were to zero the |EOS| confidence or to sample block by block.

lessons.title: Build it: turn your GPT into a masked diffusion LM

blocks.md: Time to build one. Your GPT already has everything a masked diffusion LM needs except three details (plus one practical fix you will meet below). Take the character 'h' in 'the': your GPT predicts it from 't' alone, the output at position 1 is trained against the character at position 2, and there is no way to say 'this character is unknown'. A mask predictor needs a [MASK] symbol, attention that also sees 'e' on the right, and an output at each position that guesses the character *at* that position. We make those changes, train both models on the same data for the same number of steps, and measure what lessons 3 and 4 claimed.

blocks.md: Both models use the same network: 6 layers, 6 heads, 192-dimensional embeddings, 2.68 million parameters, a 128-character context and dropout 0.2 (the value nanoGPT's Shakespeare character config uses). Both train on character-level tiny Shakespeare (the first 90% for training, the rest for validation) for 3,000 AdamW steps of 64 windows, with a peak learning rate of 0.001, 100 warmup steps and cosine decay. On an Apple-silicon laptop GPU (PyTorch's MPS backend) the GPT took 263 s and the diffusion LM 286 s, evaluations included.

The first attempt kept the GPT's learned position table (wpe). The diffusion model stalled: after 5,000 steps its bound was 2.94 nats per character against the GPT's 1.52. Swapping in rotary position embeddings (RoPE), which LLaDA uses, fixed it: with RoPE the bound reached 1.96 after only 3,000 steps.

blocks.code:
@torch.no_grad()
def generate(model, n, L=128, steps=32, remasking='low_confidence',
             temp=1.0, block_length=None):
    x = torch.full((n, L), MASK)
    block_length = block_length or L
    nb = L // block_length
    spb = steps // nb                      # steps per block
    for b in range(nb):
        lo, hi = b * block_length, (b + 1) * block_length
        k = [block_length // spb + (i < block_length % spb) for i in range(spb)]
        for i in range(spb):
            logits = model(x)
            logits[..., MASK] = -float('inf')     # never predict [MASK]
            g = -torch.log(-torch.log(torch.rand_like(logits)))
            x0 = (logits / temp + g).argmax(-1)   # Gumbel-max sample
            p = logits.softmax(-1).gather(-1, x0[..., None]).squeeze(-1)
            conf = p if remasking == 'low_confidence' else torch.rand_like(p)
            conf = torch.where(x == MASK, conf, -float('inf'))
            conf[:, hi:] = -float('inf')          # later blocks wait
            idx = conf.topk(k[i], dim=1).indices  # commit k[i] tokens
            x.scatter_(1, idx, x0.gather(1, idx))
    return x
blocks.caption: Lesson 4's sampler for a batch, following LLaDA's generate.py: k tokens per step as evenly as possible, only masked positions compete, committed tokens never change, and block_length gives semi-autoregressive sampling. Gumbel noise plus argmax samples from softmax(logits / temp).

blocks.md: Comparing the two models needs one metric. For the GPT it is the exact negative log-likelihood per character: one forward pass, the chain rule, done. For the diffusion LM we only have the bound, estimated with lesson 3's exact-count form: draw $l$ uniformly from 1 to $L$, mask exactly $l$ positions, sum the masked losses, multiply by $L/l$, and average 128 such draws. To score the same thing, both models see the first character of each 128-character validation window and are scored on the other 127.

blocks.code:
@torch.no_grad()
def mdm_bound(model, X, draws=128):         # X: (N, 128) windows
    N, L = X.shape[0], X.shape[1] - 1       # char 0 stays visible
    tot = torch.zeros(N)
    for _ in range(draws):
        l = torch.randint(1, L + 1, (N, 1))             # how many to mask
        rank = torch.rand(N, L).argsort(1).argsort(1)   # random order
        m = torch.cat([torch.zeros(N, 1, dtype=torch.bool), rank < l], 1)
        ce = F.cross_entropy(model(torch.where(m, MASK, X)).transpose(1, 2),
                             X, reduction='none')
        tot += (ce * m).sum(1) * L / l.squeeze(1)       # weight L / l
    return (tot / draws / L).mean()                     # nats per char
blocks.caption: The exact-count estimator. Averaged over draws it is an upper bound on the negative log-likelihood of the 127 characters.

blocks.prompt: After 3,000 steps, which number is lower: the GPT's exact negative log-likelihood per character or the diffusion LM's bound, and by roughly how much?
blocks.reveal: The GPT wins clearly: **1.462** nats per character exact, against a bound of **1.963** for the diffusion LM, 0.50 nats or about 34% worse (256 validation windows, 128 mask draws each). Part of the gap is the bound being loose, part is the harder task: the diffusion model must predict every character from every subset of the others, not just from its left. That is in line with lesson 7's report that masked diffusion needs about 16 times the compute for the same likelihood, though one small toy run cannot measure that factor.

blocks.md: Two lessons from the run. First, quality falls as more tokens are committed per pass, as lessons 4 and 6 said: at 16 characters per pass both samplers produce near-words, at one per pass the low-confidence sampler writes real words. Second, the judge's score alone misleads. Low-confidence remasking at 128 steps scores 1.447, almost real text's 1.413, by committing the most predictable characters first, which drives it into loops like 'your your your'. Splitting the canvas into 4 blocks of 32 (32 steps in total) traded some of that back: judge NLL 2.441 and diversity 0.390, against 1.934 and 0.211 for the whole canvas at 32 steps. This is why papers report a score that also counts diversity, such as MAUVE in lesson 8.

Three edits turn a GPT into a masked diffusion LM: a [MASK] id, `is_causal=False`, and targets at the same positions as the inputs. In practice add a fourth, relative positions such as RoPE, so the bidirectional model learns locality quickly. At equal size and steps it trains to a worse likelihood than the GPT, and its samples get better as each pass commits fewer tokens.

blocks.question: A learner trains the diffusion model but forgets change 3, keeping the AR loader whose targets are the inputs shifted by one. Attention is bidirectional. What does training do?
options: It works the same, since the shift does not matter
Wherever the next character is visible the model just copies it, so the loss falls without real learning, and outputs no longer predict their own positions as the sampler expects
Training fails with a shape error
It becomes an ordinary autoregressive model
blocks.explain: With full attention and a target of x[i+1] at position i, the answer sits in the input one position to the right whenever that position is visible. The model learns to copy its neighbour. Causal attention is what makes the shifted target a real prediction task. DiffuLLaMA's shift in lesson 8 is different: output i is scored only when position i+1 itself is masked, so nothing leaks.

blocks.question: In the run, low-confidence remasking at 128 steps reached a judge NLL of 1.447, close to real text's 1.413. What is the best reading?
options: The diffusion samples are now as good as real Shakespeare

The sampler commits the most predictable characters first and falls into repetition (diversity 0.111 against 0.516), which a judge model rewards, so the score overstates quality
More steps make diffusion samples worse
blocks.explain: A likelihood judge prefers predictable text, and repetition is predictable. The low diversity shows the samples are not like real text even though the judge scores them well. Random remasking is the exact reverse process; it is worse here because this small model's per-position marginals are poor, not because of a bug.

lessons.title: Why parallel decoding breaks, and how to make it fast

blocks.md: If one pass can fill eight masks, why not fill all 256 in one pass? Because the model outputs a separate distribution for each masked position, all computed from the same input. Sampling several positions in one step draws each from its own **marginal** (the distribution of that one position on its own, ignoring what the other positions will become), as if they were independent given what is visible. Real text is full of dependencies between neighbouring tokens.

blocks.prompt: Prompt: 'The list of poker hands that consist of two English words are: __ __'. The true answers are equally likely: 'high card', 'two pair', 'full house', 'straight flush'. If a model knows each position's marginal exactly and fills both blanks in one step, how often is the pair a real hand?
blocks.reveal: Each blank's marginal is uniform over 4 words, so the product of marginals spreads probability 1/16 over all 16 combinations. Only 4 combinations are real hands: 4 x 1/16 = 0.25. Three times in four you get nonsense like 'high house'. This example comes from Song and Zhou and is used in the Fast-dLLM paper (Wu et al., 2025), a method for speeding up diffusion LLMs covered below.

blocks.title: True joint vs product of marginals for two blanks

scenes.caption: The true joint distribution: each real hand has probability 0.25 and mixed pairs have 0.
Product of marginals: each real hand gets 0.0625 and the 12 mixed pairs share 0.75. The coherent total is 0.25.
Fill one blank per step instead: after 'full' is committed, the next pass sees it and puts all its mass on 'house'. Sequential steps restore the dependency, at the cost of an extra pass.

blocks.tex: \underbrace{p(x^i \mid x_t)\, p(x^j \mid x_t)}_{\text{what parallel decoding samples}} \;\ne\; \underbrace{p(x^i \mid x_t)\, p(x^j \mid x_t, x^i)}_{\text{the true joint}}
blocks.caption: The conditional independence assumption behind parallel unmasking. Parallel decoding samples each token from its own marginal; the true joint picks the second token given the first. The more tokens unmasked in one step, the larger the mismatch can be.

blocks.md: When is parallel decoding safe? Fast-dLLM proves a clean condition. Suppose each of $n$ positions has a top token with marginal probability above $1 - \epsilon$. If $\epsilon \le \frac{1}{n+1}$, then the greedy choice from the product of marginals equals the greedy choice from the true joint, and the bound is tight. The reasoning takes three steps. By the union bound, the chance that at least one of the $n$ positions is not its top token is below $n\epsilon$, so the combination of all top tokens has joint probability above $1 - n\epsilon$. Any other combination differs in some position, where its token has marginal probability below $\epsilon$, so its joint probability is below $\epsilon$. The top combination therefore wins whenever $1 - n\epsilon \ge \epsilon$, which rearranges to $\epsilon \le \frac{1}{n+1}$. Confident tokens can be committed together; uncertain ones should wait.

blocks.title: Confidence needed to unmask n tokens at once

scenes.caption: From the Fast-dLLM theorem: committing n tokens in one step is guaranteed to match greedy sequential decoding when every one of them has confidence above 1 - 1/(n+1). Ten tokens at once need more than 10/11, about 0.909, each.

blocks.md: This motivates **confidence-aware parallel decoding**: instead of a fixed number of tokens per step, commit every masked token whose confidence exceeds a threshold, and always commit at least the single most confident one so the loop makes progress. Easy stretches (boilerplate, closing brackets, |EOS| runs) go many tokens at a time; hard stretches go one at a time.

The second obstacle is the **KV cache**. In a causal model, a token's keys and values never change once computed, so they can be stored. With bidirectional attention, every key and value depends on every other token, including masks that are about to be filled. An exact cache is impossible, so LLaDA recomputes the entire sequence on every step.

Fast-dLLM observed that keys and values barely change between adjacent steps (cosine similarity near 1, meaning the old and new vectors point in almost the same direction) and caches them approximately. Generation proceeds block by block; the prompt and finished blocks are cached and refreshed once per block. **DualCache** also caches the all-mask suffix, so a step only recomputes the current block. The results below are on GSM8K 5-shot (five solved examples placed in the prompt before each question) on one NVIDIA A100 GPU.

blocks.md: Diffusion decoding uses fewer sequential passes but more total compute per answer. It wins wall-clock time only when each pass is memory-bound (small batches, interactive latency): lesson 1's estimate gives an H100 room for about 295 tokens per pass at the cost of one. Caching and confidence thresholds exist to shrink the compute overhead without giving back the parallelism.

Do not read 'parallel generation' as 'all tokens in one step'. Quality drops quickly when many interdependent tokens are committed together; useful systems unmask a few to a few dozen tokens per pass depending on confidence.

blocks.question: You set Fast-dLLM's threshold so that, in a hard reasoning span, no masked token reaches it. What does the sampler do?
options: It commits the single most confident token, so it degrades gracefully to one token per pass
It stalls until the model becomes more confident
It commits every token in the block anyway
It restarts the block with a new random seed
blocks.explain: The threshold rule always unmasks the highest-confidence token to guarantee progress. In uncertain regions the sampler becomes sequential, which is exactly where dependencies between tokens matter most.

blocks.question: Why can a diffusion LM not use an exact KV cache the way a GPT does?
options: Its vocabulary is too large
It uses grouped-query attention
Bidirectional attention makes every position's keys and values depend on all other positions, which change whenever a mask is filled
Diffusion models have no keys or values
blocks.explain: In a causal model, later tokens never affect earlier keys and values, so caching is exact. Without the causal mask, filling any position changes every layer's activations everywhere. Fast-dLLM reuses them approximately because adjacent steps change them very little.

lessons.title: Where diffusion LMs stand: results, block diffusion, and limits

blocks.md: The idea took several steps to become competitive. D3PM (Austin et al., 2021) generalized discrete diffusion to structured transition matrices (tables that give, for every token, the probability of turning into each other token in one forward step), including absorbing-state masking. SEDD (Score Entropy Discrete Diffusion, Lou et al., 2023) learns ratios of probabilities between a sequence and the same sequence with one token changed, the discrete counterpart of the score (the gradient of the log-probability) that image diffusion learns; it trains them with a loss it calls score entropy, and was competitive with GPT-2 on perplexity. MDLM (Sahoo et al., 2024) showed that a simple masked objective with good engineering narrows the gap further. LLaDA (Nie et al., 2025) scaled masked diffusion to 8B parameters trained from scratch.

That line is all discrete. A parallel branch ran diffusion on continuous vectors. **Diffusion-LM** (Li et al., 2022) maps each word to a learned embedding vector, adds Gaussian noise to the vectors as image diffusion does to pixels, learns to remove it, and ends with a learned **rounding** step that turns each denoised vector back into a word. Its aim was control: continuous intermediate states let gradients from a classifier steer the text toward, say, a target syntax. The paper lists the costs: a worse likelihood bound than an equal autoregressive Transformer (3.88 against 3.05 nats per token on ROCStories, a set of five-sentence everyday stories; lower is better), decoding that was 7 times slower even at 200 steps, and slower training.

Discrete diffusion itself comes in two flavours of noise. **Absorbing** noise replaces tokens with [MASK]. **Uniform** noise replaces them with random real tokens, so a corrupted position looks like an ordinary word and the model must also decide which tokens are wrong. SEDD trained both: at GPT-2 small scale its perplexity bound on LAMBADA (passages whose last word needs the whole passage to guess) was 50.92 with absorbing noise and 65.40 with uniform noise. Masking won on likelihood and on simplicity, and every result in this course is for masking.

Its base model is close to LLaMA3 8B Base overall, which saw about 15 trillion tokens, and is stronger on math and Chinese tasks while weaker on several general benchmarks. The comparison uses standard test sets: MMLU (Massive Multitask Language Understanding, multiple-choice questions on 57 subjects), BBH (BIG-Bench Hard, 23 hard reasoning tasks), HellaSwag (pick the most sensible ending of a short everyday scene), HumanEval (write 164 Python functions, checked by unit tests), and GSM8K and Math from lesson 4.

blocks.md: **Mercury** (Inception Labs, 2025) is a commercial diffusion LLM family. Its technical report describes a Transformer trained with a diffusion loss on the order of trillions of tokens and served by a proprietary engine with custom kernels and dynamic batching; the training details are not public. Independent measurements of the API endpoints in early 2025 by Artificial Analysis, a company that benchmarks AI models and the APIs that serve them, put Mercury Coder Mini at 1109 and Small at 737 output tokens per second on H100s (NVIDIA data-center GPUs). Quality in the next figure is HumanEval pass@1: the fraction of HumanEval's 164 Python problems whose first generated solution passes the unit tests. LiveCodeBench is a harder coding benchmark that keeps adding newly published contest problems, so models are less likely to have seen them in training.

blocks.md: **Block diffusion** (BD3-LM, short for Block Discrete Denoising Diffusion Language Model, Arriola et al., 2025) makes the semi-autoregressive idea part of training. The sequence is split into blocks of size $L'$; the model is autoregressive across blocks and runs discrete diffusion within each block, using a block-causal attention mask: a token attends to every token in its own block and in earlier blocks, and to none in later blocks. Earlier blocks are final, so their keys and values can be cached exactly, and the model can keep producing blocks for variable-length output.

blocks.title: Block diffusion with block size 4

scenes.caption: Three blocks of 4 tokens. Only block 1 is being generated; later blocks do not exist yet in BD3-LM (LLaDA's variant fills a fixed-length canvas instead).
Inside block 1, ordinary masked diffusion: some positions are committed after the first step, others stay masked.
Block 1 is finished and frozen. Its keys and values go into an exact KV cache, just as in a GPT.
Block 2 diffuses while attending to the cached block 1. Parallelism inside the block, autoregression between blocks.
All three blocks done. Block size 1 recovers an autoregressive model; block size equal to the whole sequence recovers plain masked diffusion.

blocks.md: Smaller blocks trade parallelism for likelihood. On LM1B after 65B training tokens, BD3-LM's perplexity bound improves from 30.60 at $L'=16$ to 29.83 at 8 and 28.23 at 4, against 31.78 for MDLM and 22.83 for an autoregressive Transformer. The authors also identify the high variance of the diffusion loss as a cause of the gap and reduce it with clipped noise schedules that avoid extreme mask rates: the mask rate $t$ is drawn uniformly between $\beta$ and $\omega$, a narrower range than 0 to 1, so almost-empty and almost-full masks, whose losses vary the most, are not sampled.

**Open limitations.**
- The response length must be chosen before sampling (LLaDA reports low sensitivity, but it is still a fixed canvas).
- No exact KV cache for full bidirectional models; caching is approximate or needs block structure.
- Quality drops as more interdependent tokens are committed per step.
- Likelihood still lags: a scaling-law study by Nie et al. estimated masked diffusion needs about 16 times the compute of an autoregressive model for the same likelihood, though downstream tasks can tell a different story.
- Post-training is harder: GRPO and DPO, the reinforcement-learning and preference-tuning recipes that lesson 8 introduces, need the log-probability of a whole response, and a diffusion LM only has the lesson 3 bound.
- The standard sampler never revises a committed token.

Lesson 8 covers the methods that work around the last two.

Diffusion LMs fit latency-sensitive, decode-heavy work where output can be refined globally: code completion and infilling (writing the missing code between a given prefix and suffix, called fill-in-the-middle; Mercury leads its fill-in-the-middle table), editing, and tasks that need context from both sides. For maximum quality per training FLOP or long free-form generation, autoregressive models remain the default.

blocks.question: A team needs exact KV caching and variable-length outputs but wants some parallel decoding. Which design fits best?
options: Pure masked diffusion over a fixed 1024-token canvas
BERT with a 15% masking ratio
An autoregressive model sampled at high temperature
Block diffusion with a small block size, autoregressive across blocks
blocks.explain: Block diffusion freezes finished blocks, so their keys and values are cached exactly and generation can continue block after block. Diffusion inside each block still commits several tokens per pass. A fixed canvas has neither property, and BERT cannot sample text.

blocks.question: LLaDA 8B Instruct beats GPT-4o on reversal poem completion but loses badly on forward completion. What is the best reading?
options: Training to predict tokens from both sides removes the directional bias, while GPT-4o's much larger training gives it a big edge in the direction it was trained on
LLaDA is a stronger model overall
The benchmark is broken because the scores do not add to 100
GPT-4o was evaluated with a causal mask removed
blocks.explain: LLaDA's forward and reversal scores are close (51.8 vs 45.6) because its objective covers all conditioning directions. GPT-4o is far stronger in the forward direction (82.7) but falls to 34.3 in reverse, the reversal curse. Neither result says LLaDA is better overall.

lessons.title: Making diffusion LMs useful: AR initialization, RL and remasking

blocks.md: LLaDA trained 8 billion parameters from scratch on 2.3 trillion tokens. Meanwhile there are many strong autoregressive checkpoints whose weights already know grammar, facts and code. In lesson 5 you turned your GPT into a diffusion LM by flipping `is_causal` and dropping the shift, then trained from random weights. What if you had kept the trained GPT weights instead? This lesson covers three things that made diffusion LMs practical after LLaDA: starting from an autoregressive model, reinforcement learning and preference tuning without an exact likelihood, and samplers that can take a token back.

**Adaptation** (Gong et al., 2024) converts autoregressive checkpoints into diffusion models by continued pre-training. DiffuGPT starts from GPT-2 (127M and 355M parameters) and DiffuLLaMA from LLaMA 2 7B, using under 200 billion tokens of training. Two tricks close the gap between the objectives. **Attention mask annealing** removes the causal mask gradually instead of at once (10,000 steps for DiffuGPT; the 7B model switched to full attention directly for efficiency). The **shift operation** keeps the autoregressive habit that the hidden state at position $i$ predicts the token at $i+1$: a masked token is predicted from the output one position to its left, so the pretrained output head keeps doing the job it learned.

blocks.title: Which output predicts which token

scenes.caption: Your GPT: the output at position i is trained to predict the token at i + 1, using only positions up to i.
Lesson 5's diffusion LM: no shift. The output at a masked position predicts the token at that same position, so the trained head must relearn its job.

Adapted models (DiffuLLaMA, Dream): keep the shift. The masked token at position 3 is read from output 2, and the one at 5 from output 4, as the GPT head already does, but now with attention in both directions.

blocks.md: **Dream 7B** (Ye et al., 2025) takes the same route at a larger scale: it copies the configuration and weights of Qwen2.5 7B (Alibaba's open-weight autoregressive model), keeps the shift, and trains on 580 billion tokens. It adds **context-adaptive token-level noise rescheduling** (CART): instead of one noise level $t$ for the whole sequence, each masked token gets its own weight in the loss according to how much clean context sits near it. Compared with LLaDA, trained from scratch on about four times as many tokens, Dream reports gains across its evaluation; in a 1B-scale ablation the AR-initialized model kept a lower loss than one trained from scratch for all 200 billion tokens. The figure uses ARC-C (the hard set of the AI2 Reasoning Challenge, grade-school science questions) and two planning puzzles: Sudoku, and Countdown, combining given numbers with arithmetic to hit a target.

blocks.title: Dream 7B vs LLaDA 8B base models (Dream's evaluation)

scenes.caption: LLaDA 8B Base as evaluated in the Dream paper (its GSM8K, 70.9, differs slightly from LLaDA's own 70.3 because of the evaluation setup).
Dream 7B, initialized from Qwen2.5 7B and trained on 0.6T instead of 2.3T tokens. The largest jump is on Sudoku, a planning task where context on both sides helps.

blocks.md: Now post-training, where the model being tuned is called the **policy** $\pi_\theta$. **GRPO** (Group Relative Policy Optimization), a reinforcement learning recipe, samples several answers per prompt, scores each with a reward, and weights each answer's log-probability $\log \pi_\theta(y \mid x)$ by how much better than its group it scored. **DPO** (Direct Preference Optimization) pushes up $\log \pi_\theta(y_w \mid x) - \log \pi_{\text{ref}}(y_w \mid x)$ for the preferred answer $y_w$, where $\pi_{\text{ref}}$ is a frozen copy of the starting model, and down for the rejected one. An autoregressive model gets every one of these log-probabilities exactly from one forward pass by the chain rule. A diffusion LM has no chain rule: its sampler composed many passes in a data-dependent order, and the only handle on $\log \pi_\theta(y \mid x)$ is the lesson 3 bound, estimated by Monte Carlo over random masks. LLaDA used 128 masked samples per estimate for evaluation, far too many forward passes to backpropagate through in an RL loop.

**d1** (Zhao et al., 2025) post-trains LLaDA 8B Instruct in two stages: masked SFT on reasoning traces, then **diffu-GRPO**. MATH500, in the figure below, is a 500-problem subset of the Math benchmark. Its log-probability estimate is deliberately crude. The sequence log-probability is taken as the sum of per-token log-probabilities (a **mean-field** approximation, which treats the tokens as independent). Each per-token log-probability comes from a single forward pass with the whole answer masked and the prompt's tokens randomly masked with probability $p_{\text{mask}}$ (0.15 in their runs). A fresh prompt mask on every gradient step gives a slightly different view of the same answers, which acts as regularization and lets the method take many gradient steps per batch of expensive generations.

Masked SFT alone helps math a little and hurts Countdown (14.5).
diffu-GRPO alone beats SFT on every task.
SFT then diffu-GRPO (d1-LLaDA): the best here on all four. Planning tasks gain the most: Countdown 19.5 to 32.0, Sudoku 6.7 to 16.7.

blocks.md: **LLaDA 1.5** (Zhu et al., 2025) attacks the noise in the estimate instead. For DPO it replaces each log-likelihood with an ELBO estimate (the **evidence lower bound**: minus the lesson 3 loss, a lower bound on $\log \pi$). The estimate is random because the timesteps and masks are random. The paper proves that the bias and variance of the resulting DPO loss and gradient are bounded by the variance of the estimated preference score, so it lowers that variance in three ways: more samples per estimate ($n = 8$, which costs $n$ times the compute), spending them on $n$ different timesteps with one mask each, and **antithetic sampling**, using the same timesteps and masks for the policy and the reference model.

blocks.tex: \mathrm{Var}(\hat B_\theta - \hat B_{\text{ref}}) = \mathrm{Var}(\hat B_\theta) + \mathrm{Var}(\hat B_{\text{ref}}) - 2\,\mathrm{Cov}(\hat B_\theta, \hat B_{\text{ref}})
blocks.caption: DPO only needs the difference of two ELBO estimates for the same answer. If both use the same masks, their errors move together, the covariance is large, and most of the noise cancels in the difference.

blocks.prompt: Take lesson 5's trained toy model as the reference and a copy fine-tuned for 200 more steps as the policy. Estimate the log-ratio of one 127-character answer with one mask draw per model. How much smaller is the spread when both models share the mask than when each draws its own?
blocks.reveal: About 12 times smaller. Over 300 repeats the shared estimates average about 5 nats, the real gap between the two models. With independent masks a single draw per model has a standard deviation of **124.6** nats, about 25 times that signal; sharing the mask cuts it to **10.3**, at no extra cost. Each ELBO alone still swings by about 87 nats, but the two models' errors move together and cancel.

blocks.title: Spread of the estimated log-ratio (toy, 300 repeats)

scenes.caption: One mask draw per estimate: 124.6 nats of spread with independent masks against 10.3 with a shared mask, for a log-ratio near 5 nats. A single unshared sample is mostly noise.

Eight timesteps with one mask each: 44.6 independent, 4.7 shared. Spending the same 8 forward passes on one timestep with 8 masks gave 5.7 shared, so spreading over timesteps helps too, as VRPO's analysis says.

blocks.md: At LLaDA scale the effect is the same. In the paper's ablation with a budget of 4, the variance of the preference score was 2.2 with antithetic sampling and 2183.7 without; four timesteps with one mask each gave 2.2, against 7.3 for one timestep with four masks. Trained on 350,000 preference pairs, LLaDA 1.5 improved on LLaDA 8B Instruct by 4.7 points on GSM8K (78.6 to 83.3), 3.0 on HumanEval and 4.0 on IFEval (a test of following checkable instructions, such as a word limit), while naive DPO with a single unshared sample gained only 2.1 on GSM8K and lost 1.2 on HumanEval.

Last, revising tokens. In the standard sampler a committed token is final, since the exact reverse step carries visible tokens over with probability 1. **ReMDM** (Wang et al., 2025) derives a different backward process with the same marginals: at each step a visible token is put back to [MASK] with probability $\sigma_t$, and masked tokens are revealed a little more often to compensate, so the expected fraction visible still matches the forward process at every time. Write $\alpha_t = 1 - t$ for the fraction visible at time $t$. To keep the probabilities valid, $\sigma_t$ may be at most $\min\{1, (1-\alpha_s)/\alpha_t\}$, and $\sigma_t = 0$ gives back the ordinary sampler. Its training loss is a reweighted MDLM loss, so the sampler runs on an already trained model.

blocks.tex: P(\text{remask a visible token}) = \sigma_t, \qquad P(\text{reveal a masked token}) = \frac{\alpha_s - (1-\sigma_t)\,\alpha_t}{1 - \alpha_t}
blocks.caption: ReMDM's step from t to s (Algorithm 1 of the paper, in this course's notation). With t = 0.5, s = 0.25 and sigma = 0.25: remask with probability 0.25, reveal with probability (0.75 - 0.375) / 0.5 = 0.75.

blocks.title: One ReMDM step: t = 0.5 to s = 0.25, sigma = 0.25

scenes.caption: Eight positions, four visible and four masked, the expected state at t = 0.5. The ordinary step would reveal 2 of the 4 masks (probability 0.5 each) and touch nothing else.

ReMDM first gives each visible token a 0.25 chance of going back to [MASK]: one of four on average. Suppose it is 'dog', a wrong early guess (illustrative; ReMDM-conf makes low-confidence tokens likelier to be picked).
Each of the old masks is revealed with probability 0.75, three of four on average. The fraction visible is 0.5 x 0.75 + 0.5 x 0.75 = 0.75, exactly the forward process at s = 0.25.

The ReMDM step ended with six visible, the same count as the ordinary step, but with one earlier decision reopened. Shown here: a later step fills position 2 with 'cat' using all the context around it.

blocks.md: Because errors can be fixed, extra steps now buy quality, a form of **inference-time scaling**. The paper measures sample quality on OpenWebText (an open copy of the web text GPT-2 was trained on) with **MAUVE**, a score from 0 to 1 of how close the distribution of generated texts is to that of human texts, rather than generative perplexity (how likely a fixed AR model finds the samples), because perplexity alone can be gamed: a tuned sampler that repeats 'love love love' scored a generative perplexity of 1.5.

blocks.title: MAUVE on OpenWebText, 1024-token samples

scenes.caption: MDLM with the ordinary sampler (nucleus sampling). More steps do not help: MAUVE drifts from 0.042 to 0.035.
ReMDM on the same kind of model: 0.403, 0.610, 0.656, approaching the 0.760 of an autoregressive model with the same architecture.

blocks.md: The mechanism of a diffusion LM is unchanged by all three ideas. AR initialization reuses weights through the shift operation, RL and DPO replace the exact log-probability with cheap or variance-reduced estimates of the bound, and ReMDM changes only the sampler so that more steps can fix mistakes.

An estimate of the bound is not the log-probability. d1's one-pass mean-field estimate is biased by construction, and an ELBO estimate is both a bound and noisy. Methods that work here control that error (shared masks, many timesteps, random prompt masks as regularization); plugging a single random ELBO sample into an AR recipe is what LLaDA 1.5 calls naive DPO.

blocks.question: A team runs DPO on a diffusion LM and estimates each of the four ELBOs (policy and reference, chosen and rejected) with its own fresh random masks. Training is unstable. What is the cheapest fix?
options: Switch to a causal attention mask during DPO
Lower the learning rate until the noise averages out
Estimate each ELBO with a single timestep and many masks at that timestep
Use the same timesteps and masks for the policy and reference estimates of each answer
blocks.explain: Antithetic sampling costs nothing extra: the policy and reference ELBOs share their randomness, so their errors cancel in the log-ratio that DPO uses. Spending a budget on one timestep with many masks is worse than spreading it over timesteps, and a smaller step size only slows learning.

blocks.question: Why does DiffuLLaMA keep the 'shift operation' when it turns LLaMA into a diffusion model?
options: Because bidirectional attention cannot work without it
Because the shift makes the KV cache exact
So that the pretrained output at position i keeps predicting the token at i + 1, reusing what the AR weights already learned
Because masked tokens must always be predicted from the right
blocks.explain: An AR model's hidden state at i is trained to encode the next token. Keeping that alignment means a masked token is read from its left neighbour's output, so continued training starts close to what the weights already do. Attention is fully bidirectional either way, and caching is unaffected.
